newsitem.title: UK: British interest rates unchanged as inflation eases.
newsitem.headline: British interest rates unchanged as inflation eases.

text.p: The British government left official interest rates unchanged Thursday, despite recent pressure from the Bank of England for an increase, as official figures showed annual inflation fell in December.

The Office for National Statistics said retail price inflation slowed to 2.5 percent year-on-year in December from 2.7 percent in November, while the underlying rate, which excludes mortgage interest payments, dipped to 3.1 percent.

"These figures show that subdued cost pressures and a stronger pound are feeding through to lower inflation," Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke, the nation's finance minister, said in a statement.
Clarke met Bank of England Governor Eddie George Wednesday for their monthly meeting on monetary policy.

Although no statement was made after the talks, the central bank carried out routine money market operations at established rates Thursday morning, indicating that official rates remained unchanged at 6.0 percent.
The Bank has repeatedly called for an increase in interest rates in recent months because it fears inflation will head higher this year.
However, Clarke, who has the final say on monetary policy, made clear in a BBC radio interview that he was still not convinced that the economy was beginning to overheat.

"When I make decisions on interest rates, I look at how good were conditions in shops for Christmas, what is happening to production, how strong is the housing market getting," he said. "The big thing at the moment is the pound (sterling) is very strong and that is very anti-inflationary."
December retail sales appear to have been weaker than expected, while figures already released show manufacturing output actually fell last month.
The strong pound dampens inflation by making imported goods cheaper for British firms.
